questions_now.q: What does MDMA feel like?

lines_now.short: Compared with a dummy pill, lab MDMA felt good for hours, with unwanted effects too.
lines_now.but: Lab volunteers were healthy and had researchers with them; the one study at a real club was small, with no dummy pill.
how: In the biggest set of lab studies (166 healthy adults), the good effect was rated about 80 out of 100, against 3 or 4 after a dummy pill. It began in about half an hour and lasted about four hours. Looking back, 67 in 100 called it positive and 15 in 100 disappointing or bad.

The same sessions brought unwanted effects, like less appetite, a dry mouth or a clenched jaw. Some felt little: for some the start was slow, and an antidepressant given first cut the effect. Nobody took more, so that was not tested.

At a London club, people who took ecstasy felt about as good as other clubbers, most of whom were drinking. Two days later they felt sadder and less sociable than the others. A week later they felt like the others again.

In the club study, people chose their own drugs, nobody checked what was in the pills, and people rated their own moods knowing what the study was about. So it shows what they felt, not what MDMA alone did.
lines_now.rate: Lab trials in which 166 healthy volunteers each got both MDMA and a dummy pill; the gap was very large, and four places agree. Most could tell which they got, though.

claim.statement: In healthy, screened adults given MDMA by mouth by researchers in laboratories, and a placebo on another day, MDMA raised ratings of the drug's effect, of a good effect and of feeling happy, and, in one study, of feeling open and close to others, and also raised ratings of a bad effect and of physical complaints, in the same sessions (five papers from Basel, Chicago, San Francisco and Zurich, not fully independent: the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers a senior author, and one author is on four of the five). In 166 volunteers aged 18 to 45 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel, four in five new to MDMA, the average highest self-rating of 'any drug effect' on a 0 to 100 line was 73 in men and 85 in women after 125 mg (136 people), against 4 on placebo, and lower after 75 mg (30 other people); of 'good drug effect' it was 77 and 82 after 125 mg, against 3 or 4. Four of the 166 reported no effect. The effect began on average 33 minutes after the dose (SD 24), peaked at 1.6 hours (SD 0.8) and lasted 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4 to 8.2); in 16 volunteers in Zurich it began 20 to 120 minutes after the dose and lasted about 3 hours. In a 32-person Basel study (probably within the 166), ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others rose (F(1,31) 121, 81 and 68; p < 0.001), as did scores for well-being, extroversion and activity, with no rise in anxiety; in Zurich, positive mood averaged 40% of the highest possible score against 0.6% on placebo and thought disorder 25% against 0, with no rise in aggression-anger, apprehension-anxiety or depressiveness. The social effects are less settled: a 'sociable' rating rose at 1.5 mg/kg in 9 people in Chicago (+19.7 points against -6.3; p = .04, which the authors call marginal) while a friendliness scale did not change significantly; closeness was rated higher in San Francisco than in Basel; peak ratings of drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ significantly between three sites (220 volunteers, partly overlapping the others; no means printed, and no significant difference is not proof of equality); and empathy and money-sharing tests rose in one Basel study, in men only on post hoc tests. The same sessions brought unwanted effects. 'Bad drug effect' averaged 13 in men and 24 in women after 125 mg against 2 on placebo, higher in women also after allowing for dose per kilogram and blood level (SDs of 22 and 24, so ratings varied widely). In the first 6 hours, MDMA against placebo in 166 people: lack of appetite 59%, dry mouth 55%, difficulty concentrating 46%, cold feet 42%, sweating 41% and jaw clenching 40% (of 134 asked), against 0 to 6%; at 24 hours, lack of appetite 31% (1% on placebo), lack of energy 30% (3%) and headache 33% (15%). Nine people reported anxiety, all after 125 mg; the authors say verbal support reduced it and no benzodiazepine was used. The paper reports no serious adverse event, depressed mood in 4% after 125 mg in the next one to two weeks, and 'flashbacks' (not defined) in 9%, 8 to 50 hours after the dose. Asked at the end of the study, 67% of 141 volunteers called the experience positive, 18% neutral and 15% disappointing or bad; 19% would probably not take MDMA again, 47% only in another controlled study and 34% perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known. Why people take MDMA was not studied: none of the five laboratory papers asked people who use ecstasy why they do or what they feel in real use (one small study outside the laboratory, below, measured what they felt); two say, citing other papers, that sociability and empathy are reasons for recreational use. Some people feel little from an amount. Of the reasons usually given, these studies show a start that ranged up to 120 minutes in Zurich; a lowering of Zurich ratings by about 60% by an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion before MDMA; peak blood levels averaging 1.29 times higher in women than in men at the same 125 mg; and, in Chicago and less clearly San Francisco, a lower 'any drug effect' rating with more earlier MDMA use (not for other ratings, and the other way round in Basel); a pill of different content was not tested, as every capsule held a known amount. No one took a second dose within a session, so what happens when people take more was not measured here (controlled second-dose studies are covered in a separate claim). The sessions differ from real life: healthy, screened volunteers (mostly new to MDMA in Basel and Zurich; earlier use in Chicago and San Francisco) took a known capsule and nothing else, at an amount set by the researchers, in a hospital or laboratory room (22.7 degrees Celsius in Basel) with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco; in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis people were alone and gave higher 'anxious' ratings than at the other sites, which the authors suggest, untested, may reflect company. The end-of-study answers came from people given MDMA by researchers, not from people who chose it, and heat, crowds and other drugs were not part of the MDMA sessions. Outside the laboratory, one small study with no placebo followed 45 people aged 19 to 30, recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub, from a drug-free session before a Saturday night out to the club and then 2 and 7 days later: 30 who had used ecstasy before (15 of them ten or more times) took tablets of untested content by their own choice that night, and 15 who had never taken it, 10 of whom drank alcohol, went to the same club (Parrott & Lasky, 1998). At the club all three groups rated their mood as good and the ecstasy groups' ratings were not clearly better (sad 9 against 20 out of 100, p < 0.10; good tempered about the same), though they felt more 'abnormal'; the authors had expected better moods and point to the setting and expectation, the comparison group's drinking, ratings already near the top of the scale and a mood list with no items on elation or empathy. Two days later both ecstasy groups rated themselves sadder (56 and 53 against 22), more unsociable and more 'abnormal', and the novice group also more depressed, more unpleasant and less good tempered (in the regular group these three reached only p < 0.10); seven days later the groups rated these moods alike again. These are self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims and their own group, with means only, many comparisons and no correction, and sleep and drug use after the night were not recorded, so the study shows what this group reported over that week, not what MDMA alone did.
claim.population: Healthy, screened adults, aged 18 to 45 in the largest set, in research laboratories: 166 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel (83 women, 83 men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA; 30 people took 75 mg and 136 took 125 mg), 32 in a Basel study probably within them (22 new to MDMA), 16 in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 13 had never taken MDMA), 9 in Chicago with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions) and, in a three-site pooled analysis that may overlap the others, 220 (Basel 80, Chicago 95, San Francisco 45; lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions; 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory); outside the laboratory, 45 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30 recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub: 15 with ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, 15 with one to nine and 15 who had never taken it
claim.exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, given double blind by researchers in a hospital or laboratory (study conditions: 125 mg or 75 mg in Basel; 1.5 mg/kg in Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco; a fixed 125 mg in the Basel part of the three-site analysis; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order in the Chicago brain-imaging study), with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco, people alone in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis, no other drug, and ratings made at set times; in Zurich, MDMA after an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion was also tested; outside the laboratory, tablets sold as ecstasy taken by people's own choice at a club, content not tested (study condition, self-reported: 1.80 tablets on average in the regular group and 1.45 in the novice group), with alcohol, cannabis or cocaine taken by some in every group
claim.comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover; in Chicago the placebo session was placed at random among ascending doses); sites and earlier-use groups are compared across different people; in Zurich, MDMA after a citalopram infusion in the same people; outside the laboratory, people at the same club who had never taken ecstasy (10 of 15 drank alcohol that night), and each group's own drug-free session before the night
claim.outcome: Self-ratings of drug effects on 0 to 100 lines (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, feeling happy, open, close to others, sociable, stimulated, anxious) and mood and altered-state scales; time to onset, peak and end of the effect; physical complaints on a 66-item list up to 6 hours and at 24 hours; end-of-study answers on the overall experience and on taking MDMA again; empathy and money-sharing tests as secondary outcomes; outside the laboratory, 16 single-item mood self-ratings (0 to 100) before the night, at the club, and 2 and 7 days later
claim.magnitude: Basel pooled analysis (166 people; 125 mg n = 136, 75 mg n = 30), highest self-rating on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo, at 125 mg: any drug effect women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); good drug effect women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); bad drug effect women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); at 75 mg any drug effect 59 (29) and 56 (32), good 60 (28) and 57 (33), bad 35 (33) and 7 (11). Drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44 (p < 0.001); women's bad-effect ratings stayed higher after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0) and blood level (F 21.5), both p < 0.001. Four of the 166 reported no effect; onset 33 (SD 24) minutes, peak 1.6 (0.8) hours, duration 4.2 (1.3) hours (range 1.4 to 8.2). Complaints, MDMA against placebo (of 166), up to 6 hours: lack of appetite 59% against 2%, dry mouth 55% against 2%, difficulty concentrating 46% against 6%, cold feet 42% against 4%, sweating 41% against 0, jaw clenching 40% against 1% (134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, heart palpitations 24% (each 0 to 1% on placebo), nausea 11% against 1%, anxiety 9 people (printed as 6%; 9 of 166 is 5.4%, editors' calculation) against 0, headache 25% against 16% (not significant); at 24 hours: lack of appetite 31% against 1%, headache 33% against 15%, lack of energy 30% against 3%. No serious adverse event; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg; flashbacks 12 of 141 (9%) at 8 to 50 hours. End of study (141 asked): experience positive 95 (67%), neutral 25 (18%), disappointing or bad 21 (15%); would probably not take MDMA again 27 (19%), only in another controlled study 66 (47%), perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known 48 (34%). At 125 mg women's peak blood level averaged 1.29 times men's. Basel, 32 people: feeling happy F(1,31) 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52 (p < 0.001); well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, activity 24.48; anxiety not raised; empathy test explicit F 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047), men only on post hoc tests; money sharing F 4.42 (p = 0.044), men p = 0.008. Zurich, 16 people, mean % of the highest possible score (SE): positive mood 40.1 (6.6) against 0.6 on placebo; derealization 32.7 (7.0) against 0.4; thought disorder 24.8 (6.0) against 0.0; onset 20 to 120 (mean 45) minutes; about 60% lower after citalopram (authors' figure). Chicago, 9 people: 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (1.5 mg/kg against placebo p = .04, marginal); friendliness scale F 1.3, not significant. Three sites, 220 people: peak ratings of any drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ by site (p = 0.07 to 1.00; no means printed); earlier use and the any-drug-effect rating: 6.8 points lower per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7), 13.5 higher in Basel (CI 1.63 to 25.3; fewer than three earlier uses). Outside the laboratory (Parrott & Lasky, 1998; 15 people per group; 0 to 100 self-ratings, means only; Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group): at the club good tempered 85 (comparison), 90 (novice) and 88 (regular); sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); 2 days later sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); 7 days later none of these differed (sad 22, 25 and 21; depressed 37, 37 and 39). Group by session interactions: p < 0.001 for sad, depressed and abnormal; p < 0.01 for unsociable and unpleasant; p < 0.05 for good tempered.
claim.rating_reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that, in healthy volunteers in laboratory sessions, a single dose of MDMA raised self-rated drug effect and good effect above placebo (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 at 125 mg, in 136 people), began within about an hour, lasted about four hours, and was accompanied by bad-effect ratings and physical complaints in the same sessions. The parts that rest on one small study or on marginal or post hoc tests (sociability in 9 people, the empathy and money-sharing tests, face recognition, the earlier-use relation, the effect of citalopram) are worded as such and would be rated lower on their own; a separate claim could carry them. The certainty does not extend to real use or to why people take MDMA, which the laboratory studies did not measure. The real-life sentences rest on one observational study of 45 people with no placebo, self-chosen tablets of untested content, unblinded self-ratings and no spread printed (ROBINS-E very high on its study card); they qualify the claim and are not part of the moderate rating, and on their own would be very low (observational start, risk of bias -2, imprecision -1). Status replicated: the direction agrees at four places, but the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers share a senior author and one author (Liechti) is on four of the five papers (the Basel pooled paper, the Basel empathy paper, the Zurich paper and the three-site paper, which also includes the Chicago senior author), so the four places are not fully independent. The claim gives no advice on amounts or timing, and describing the effects people rated as good is a finding, not encouragement.

questions_now.q: Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?
Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?

lines_now.short: In one large study, the risk of dying was highest 2 to 7 days after release.
lines_now.but: The records did not name the drugs, and no one measured tolerance.
how: Researchers used death records for about 1.5 million people who left prison or jail. They lived in eight countries, from 1980 to 2018.
16 of the 18 groups had records for each day. In them, the risk of dying in days 2 to 7 after release was about 1.5 to 2 times the risk in later weeks.
Poisoning by alcohol or other drugs was the most common recorded cause of death, in that first week and overall. But 91 in 100 of these deaths happened more than 4 weeks after release.
The study had no information on drug use, treatment or tolerance. So it cannot say why the first week is riskier.
lines_now.rate: Death records of 1,471,526 people released from prison or jail in eight countries, all analysed the same way. But it is one study, and how causes were recorded wasn't checked.

claim.statement: In people released from prison or jail in eight mostly high-income countries between 1980 and 2018, the death rate was highest in the first week after release (counted from day 2), and deaths coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in that week, although most such deaths happened later. In 18 record-linkage cohorts of everyone released (1,471,526 people, 88.3% of them men, in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 75,427 deaths), the pooled crude death rate over the whole follow-up was 725 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 625 to 831). The analyses by time since release used the 16 cohorts, in seven countries, that could give deaths by day (New Zealand's only cohort and one from Washington State could not): the rate was 1,612 (1,048 to 2,287) in days 2 to 7 after release and 737 (636 to 844) more than a year after release, and the first week's rate was 1.5 times that of the second week (1.2 to 1.8), 2.0 times that of weeks 3–4 (1.5 to 2.6) and 2.2 times that of weeks 9–12 (1.6 to 3.0). The 'first week' starts on day 2 because, by the authors' reading of their data, deaths in custody may have been recorded in some cohorts as deaths on the day of release, probably inflating the release-day rate (4,036 per 100,000 person-years; 826, with an interval of 0 to 3,455, in the ten cohorts that could separate the two). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning, of unintentional or undetermined intent, a single category that does not separate alcohol, other drugs or combinations and names no drug, had a rate of 657 (332 to 1,076) in days 2 to 7, above suicide (135) and heart and blood vessel disease (71), and of 146 (103 to 197) over the whole follow-up, where they were the leading cause (16,126 deaths, 21.4%); yet 14,671 of these 16,126 deaths (91.0%) happened more than 4 weeks after release (Borschmann et al., 2024; the paper does not say whether counted from the first release in the study period or from the latest one), since most of the time people were followed lies beyond the first weeks (the editors' explanation). The study compared periods after release with one another, not with the general population; rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1,183 per 100,000 person-years over the whole follow-up) and regions (days 2 to 7: Europe 2,762, the USA 934); causes came from death registers, and the paper reports no check of how deaths were certified or coded across countries and decades; and it analysed only age and sex, with no information on what happened between release and death, so it says nothing about drug use, treatment in custody or tolerance and cannot show why deaths cluster soon after release. Whether, and how fast, tolerance falls during a break from opioids is a separate answer, which rests on reviews (see the answer on tolerance after a break from opioids). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claim.population: People released from incarceration (prison or jail) in 18 cohorts of everyone released in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA, 1980–2018 (1,471,526 people; 88.3% men); analyses by time since release in the 16 cohorts, in seven countries, that could give deaths by day
claim.exposure: Time since release (days 2–7, week 2, weeks 3–4, weeks 9–12, more than a year)
claim.comparator: Later periods after release in the same cohorts (no comparison with the general population)
claim.outcome: Crude death rates per 100,000 person-years, all causes and by underlying cause coded in death registers (alcohol and other drug poisoning of unintentional or undetermined intent; suicide; cardiovascular disease)
claim.magnitude: Borschmann et al. (2024), pooled crude rates per 100,000 person-years: all causes, whole follow-up 725 (95% CI 625–831), 18 cohorts; days 2–7 1612 (1048–2287), I² 91.1%, and more than 1 year 737 (636–844), from the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day, as are all the period-specific figures below; first week vs week 2 IRR 1.5 (1.2–1.8), vs weeks 3–4 2.0 (1.5–2.6), vs weeks 9–12 2.2 (1.6–3.0). Days 2–7 by cause: alcohol and other drug poisoning 657 (332–1076), suicide 135 (36–277), cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). Whole follow-up: poisoning 146 (103–197), 16,126 of 75,427 deaths (21.4%); 14,671 of the 16,126 (91.0%) more than 4 weeks after release (from which release is not stated). Release day 4036 (887–8940), 826 (0–3455) in the ten cohorts that separated deaths in custody. Cohorts 236 to 1183; days 2–7 Europe 2762 (1832–3872), USA 934 (389–1703). Excluding time back in custody (16 cohorts) 720 (605–845).
claim.rating_reasoning: Descriptive (crude death rates by time since release): starts low; not downgraded and not upgraded (descriptive claims are never upgraded). The rating applies to the all-cause pattern; the poisoning figures, taken alone, would be rated very low for risk of bias (unappraised cause-of-death coding across countries and decades), and the statement labels them as coded causes that name no drug. The rates by time since release come from the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day (Figure 2), which the statement says and which does not change the rating. Status single study: one individual participant data meta-analysis; the cohort-by-cohort results by time since release are in the appendix, which was not read, so the 18 cohorts are not counted as independent replications here, and earlier studies of deaths after release (for example Binswanger et al., 2007, whose Washington cohort is one of the 18) were not read. The first-week peak and the 91.0% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks hold together because most person-time lies beyond the first weeks (study card note; the editors' explanation in the statement). Nothing about tolerance was measured, and the claim does not attribute the early peak to it.

lines_now.short: About 3 in 4 people at harm reduction sites had used alone that week. The top reason was comfort at home.
lines_now.but: It was one survey in one part of Canada. Everyone asked already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, did a short survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone were more often without a steady home than people who did not.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.
lines_now.rate: One survey of 414 people who happened to visit harm reduction sites in British Columbia in 2018. 'Alone' was never defined for them, and reasons were picked from a short list.

freq.what: had used drugs alone at least once in the past week
freq.note: 314 of 414 people at 27 harm reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, in 2018.

claim.statement: In clients of 27 harm reduction supply sites across British Columbia, Canada, surveyed in 2018 (414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, recruited by convenience at the sites), 314 (75.8%; editors' 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%) said they had used drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than a quarter of the time, answering one question that did not define alone (Papamihali et al., 2020). Offered a short list of reasons, with more than one allowed, the 314 most often chose that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home (139, 44.3%; 52.7% of the 264 who gave a reason, editors' calculation), then not wanting others to know (44, 14.0%; more often under age 50 than at 50 or older, 16.9% against 5.3%) and that it is safer to be alone (30, 9.6%). Two more reasons were not on the list but were coded by the authors from written answers: having no one to use with (37, 11.7%) and not wanting to share or it being cheaper (27, 8.6%); because they could be given only in writing, their shares cannot be ranked against the listed options and may be undercounts. Written answers also included having no access to an overdose prevention site and not being allowed to use in a transition home. People who used alone more often had no regular housing (37.6% against 24.0% of those who did not use alone; adjusted odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27, in 306 people with complete answers) and more often had used crack or cocaine in the past week (41.4% against 26.0%; 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82). They also more often reported an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months (22.9% against 15.0%), but not significantly after adjustment (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69); both were reported by the same people at one sitting, so this is an association, not a prediction, and the survey cannot say whether using alone changes the risk of overdose. Coroners' reports cited in the paper's background, not data of this study, found that 69% of people who died of an overdose in British Columbia in 2016–2017 were using alone and that in 2019 the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths; the paper does not say how these deaths were defined or how using alone was established. People already in contact with services were surveyed, so the figures may not hold for people who use drugs and do not attend these sites. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Clients of 27 harm reduction supply distribution sites in all five health regions of British Columbia, Canada, May to August 2018: 414 people aged 19 or older who had used illicit drugs in the past 6 months (62.6% men; 34.3% not regularly housed; past-week use of opioids 70.0%, crystal methamphetamine 72.9%, crack or cocaine 37.7%, benzodiazepines 13.5%), recruited by convenience at the sites
claim.exposure: Using drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, from one self-report item (share of the time drugs were used alone, in bands, counted as any against none; alone not defined for respondents)
claim.comparator: Respondents who did not use alone in the past 7 days (100), for the correlates; none for the reasons
claim.outcome: Reasons chosen from a short list (more than one allowed, with free text, from which the authors coded two further reasons), asked only of those who used alone; characteristics associated with using alone; self-reported opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months
claim.magnitude: Used alone in the past 7 days: 314 of 414 (75.8%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%); more than 25% of the time: 198 (47.8%). Reasons (of 314): listed options: convenience and comfort at home 139 (44.3%; 52.7% of 264 giving a reason, editors' calculation), not wanting others to know 44 (14.0%), safer alone 30 (9.6%); coded by the authors from written answers: no one to use with 37 (11.7% as printed; 11.8% by editors' calculation), not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%), other reasons that could not be coded 19 (6.1%); prefer not to say 31 (9.9%), no response 19 (6.1%). Adjusted odds ratios (n = 306): no regular housing 2.27 (1.20 to 4.27); crack or cocaine 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); opioids 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88); crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88); opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69). Naloxone kit: 67.8% of those who used alone against 66.0%. Coroners' figures cited in the background: 69% of overdose deaths in 2016–2017 involved using alone; in 2019, the place of injury was a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence for 26.5%.
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low and is rated as a description of the population sampled (clients of harm reduction supply sites in British Columbia in 2018); rated down for risk of bias and, for the overdose part, indirectness, giving very low. The main finding, that most clients used alone at least sometimes, is unlikely to be reversed by these biases, but the exact share and the order of reasons depend on who was sampled and how the options were worded. The correlates are associations from a selected model. Status single study.

questions_now.q: Does music change how a psychedelic session goes?
Does music change how a psychedelic session goes?

lines_now.short: Patients said music shaped their sessions; two kinds of music made no clear difference.
lines_now.but: None of the studies we read compared music with silence, and the trial of two kinds of music had only 10 people.
how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.
Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest time to the music did not rate it as harder than others did.
lines_now.rate: One small trial of 10 people compared two playlists, not music with silence, and everyone knew which music played. The rest is what people said afterwards.

claim.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, and the one randomized comparison of two kinds of music, in 10 people, found no detectable difference, with intervals too wide to rule one out. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). In the one randomized comparison of music (Strickland et al., 2021), 10 adults who smoked (8 men; mean age 51), in an open-label pilot of psilocybin to help people stop smoking, each had one session with a Western classical playlist and one with an 'overtone-based' playlist of instruments such as singing bowls, gongs and didgeridoo, in random, counterbalanced order, wearing an eye mask and headphones, with a lower dose in the first session than in the second for all but one (study conditions; the analysis adjusted for dose). Mystical-type scores (MEQ30, self-rated at the end of each session and printed on a 0-to-1 scale) averaged 0.68 with the overtone playlist and 0.52 with the classical one, a difference of 0.16 (standardized 0.57; editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36, from rounded figures) that was not statistically significant (p = 0.107); Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores were almost the same (0.33 against 0.34; standardized difference −0.11, editors' interval about −0.73 to 0.51; p = 0.74). The data therefore fit anything from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores with the overtone playlist, and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge. About a quarter of the classical playlist's tracks were also on the overtone playlist, about an hour of each person's own chosen music was played in every session for nine of the ten (one chose none), the overtone playlist lost three tracks after the first three people, and everyone knew which music they heard. Six of the ten then chose the overtone playlist for a third session; smoking abstinence at the end of treatment (5 of 6 who chose it against 2 of 4 who chose the classical one; editors' Fisher p = 0.50) compares people who chose differently after hearing both playlists, so it cannot show an effect of the music. In a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025), the text reports 16 trials playing a set playlist through headphones, although Table 3 describes one of those trials with stereo speakers; one alternated music and silence, two allowed no music, and none compared settings; trials treating substance use, such as the smoking pilot, were outside its scope. An older study that compared five musical conditions, no music among them, during LSD sessions for alcohol use (Gaston and Eagle, 1970) is described by Strickland et al. as finding no significant differences, in a between-subject, partly non-random design without an objective clinical outcome; it has not been read here. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label psilocybin trial (19); adults who smoked, in an open-label psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot (10, with the order of two playlists randomized); and US adults who had used classic psychedelics in an online panel (613)
claim.exposure: Music played during psilocybin sessions: one standard playlist (with one exception), as patients described it a week later; a Western classical or an overtone-based playlist, in randomized order within each person; disagreeable music named as associated with a most challenging experience
claim.comparator: No study had a session without music: the other playlist in the same person (randomized comparison); patients who described the music less favourably; panel respondents who did not name the music
claim.outcome: What patients said the music did; fall in self-rated depression (QIDS) one week after; mystical-type experience (MEQ30) and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) self-rated after each session; smoking abstinence by chosen playlist; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after
claim.magnitude: Kaelen et al. (2018), n = 19: welcome influences 18 of 19, unwelcome 10 of 19; QIDS fall with music liking r = 0.60 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.83, editors'), resonance 0.59, openness 0.57; drug intensity r = 0.004 (−0.45 to 0.46). Simonsson et al. (2023): disagreeable music named by 30 of 613, not associated with challenge (beta 0.05, p = 0.19) or, imprecisely, with later thoughts or attempts of harm (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21); changing the music ticked as helpful by 99 of 613. Strickland et al. (2021), n = 10, randomized sessions 1 and 2: MEQ30 0.68 (SD 0.20) overtone against 0.52 (SD 0.21) Western classical, dz 0.57, p = 0.107 (dose-adjusted b = 0.14, p = 0.108); editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36 (dz about −0.12 to 1.23); CEQ 0.33 (SD 0.20) against 0.34 (SD 0.22), dz −0.11, p = 0.74 (editors' dz interval about −0.73 to 0.51). Abstinence by chosen playlist, not randomized: 5 of 6 (overtone) against 2 of 4 (classical) at the end of treatment and 4 of 6 against 2 of 4 at long-term follow-up (editors' Fisher p = 0.50 and 1.0).
claim.rating_reasoning: Rated from the one randomized comparison, the best evidence on whether the music itself changes a session: randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias, one for indirectness and two for imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The correlational evidence on how patients experienced the music (Kaelen et al., 2018) is very low on its own, as before (low, minus two for risk of bias and one for imprecision). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of the music nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status single study: each question rests on one small study (two genres compared in 10 people; the music experience and the fall in depression in 19 patients); the panel survey adds only null associations, one very imprecise, for music named as associated with a difficult experience. A systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found none that compared settings, music included; trials treating substance use were outside its scope. The published correction to Strickland et al. (2021; doi 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00119), read on 12 November 2026, changes only the acknowledgments, so no figure here is affected. The only comparison with a no-music condition in psychedelic sessions that these sources mention, a 1970 quasi-randomized study of LSD sessions (Gaston and Eagle), is known only from Strickland et al.'s description and has not been read. A 2025 opinion article argues against music in therapy settings and notes that no controlled study compares music with silence; it has no card.

lines_now.but: One online survey, looking back over a whole life, using questions borrowed from meditation research.
how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.

lines_now.rate: One online survey of 613 US adults from a sign-up panel, matched on only sex, age and ethnicity. Its borrowed questions gave counts that disagree, and no comparison group answered them.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had ever used a psychedelic, in one US online survey:
pairs: said they had had at least one difficult experience
said one had severely affected their ability to get through daily life
sought medical or psychological help afterwards
freq.note: 613 US adults asked once, in 2021, looking back over their whole life (251, 28 and 16 people). No one who had not used psychedelics was asked.

claim.statement: In an online panel of US adults matched to the population on sex, age and ethnicity only (Prolific, October 2021; Simonsson et al., 2023), 613 of 2,822 respondents (21.7%) had ever used a classic psychedelic (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote or San Pedro). Asked once, looking back over their whole life, 362 of the 613 (59.1%) said they had never had a challenging, difficult or distressing experience with them, 143 (23.3%) rarely, 80 (13.1%) occasionally and 28 (4.6%) regularly or frequently: 41 in 100 at least once (editors' calculation). 28 (4.6%) said their ability to function had been severely impaired, and 55 (9.0%; printed 8.9%) that impairment had lasted more than a day, 21 of them (3.4%) more than a month (editors' sum), but the two impairment questions gave counts that do not agree (176 reported some impairment, 262 gave its length). All 613, including the 362 who said they had never had one, were asked about their most challenging experience; in the days or weeks after it, 41 (6.7%) reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others, including 9 (1.5%) attempts to harm themselves, and 16 (2.6%) sought medical, psychiatric or psychological help. 350 (57.1%) reported at least one symptom lasting at least a few days that they put down to psychedelics, most often feeling anxious (36.1%) or difficulty sleeping (27.9%), but these questions, borrowed from meditation research, were not asked of people who had not used psychedelics or about times without them, so how many such symptoms would have happened anyway is unknown; 482 (78.6%) agreed, at least slightly, that they were glad to have used psychedelics. Challenging experiences were linked most often to LSD (by 31.5% of those who had used it, against 19.7% for psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT and 14.7% for mescaline, peyote or San Pedro), but how often each drug had been used was not asked. The 8 people taking lithium and the 16 taking another mood stabilizer at the time of their most challenging experience had higher odds of later harm thoughts or attempts (odds ratios 22.34, 95% CI 1.78 to 279.65, and 5.84, 1.40 to 24.34, adjusted only for the other medicines), estimates too imprecise, and too open to confounding by the conditions these medicines treat, to give a risk. In a self-selected online sample of people who had used psychedelics, 555 of 869 (64 in 100) said the experience they described had included a period of distress, difficulty or discomfort (Wood et al., 2024), a reminder that such figures depend on who is asked and how. In a prospective study that measured well-being before and after a planned psychedelic experience (Haijen et al., 2018), 85 of the 279 people who answered both surveys (30 in 100, editors' calculation) scored lower two weeks later, counting any fall however small, and they had not rated the experience as more challenging than the others (the paper gives no statistics for this comparison); many who started did not answer the later surveys, and with no comparison group the fall cannot be put down to the drug. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Adults in the United States who had ever used a classic psychedelic, in an opt-in online panel matched on sex, age and ethnicity (613 of 2,822), with a self-selected online sample and one prospective cohort for comparison
claim.exposure: Lifetime use of classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro)
claim.comparator: None for the frequencies (no group without psychedelic use answered the same questions)
claim.outcome: Challenging, difficult or distressing experiences; impaired functioning and its length; symptoms lasting days that respondents attributed to psychedelics; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others; help-seeking
claim.magnitude: Simonsson et al. (2023), of 613: never had a challenging experience 362 (59.1%); at least once 251 (40.9%, editors'); severe impairment 28 (4.6%); impairment over a day 55 (9.0%), over a month 21 (3.4%, editors'); harm thoughts or attempts 41 (6.7%), self-harm attempts 9 (1.5%); sought help 16 (2.6%); lasting symptoms attributed to psychedelics 350 (57.1%, no comparison group); glad 482 (78.6%, slightly to strongly agree). Lithium (8 people) OR 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65), other mood stabilizers (16) 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34), adjusted only for the other medicines. Wood et al. (2024): 555 of 869 (63.9%) recalled distress in the experience they described. Haijen et al. (2018): well-being lower at two weeks (any fall) in 85 of the 279 with both measurements (30.5%).
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled: starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low; never upgraded. Status single study: the frequencies come from one survey; the self-selected survey and the prospective cohort are reported as context, not as replication. The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations rest on 8 and 16 people and are confounded by indication: a signal, not an estimate.

questions_now.q: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?
What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?

lines_now.short: In 2001 Portugal stopped treating having any drug for your own use, even heroin, as a crime. Drug use rose slightly; new HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines_now.but: Treatment and other help for people who use drugs grew from 1999, so these figures cannot show what the law alone did.
how: Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.
Crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year, mostly because possession stopped counting as a crime.
lines_now.rate: National statistics before and after the law in one country, loosely compared with Spain and Italy. Treatment grew at the same time, and some counts changed method. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

freq.what: adults (aged 15 to 64) in Portugal said in 2007 that they had ever used an illegal drug
freq.note: National surveys: 7.8 in 100 in 2001 (7.6 in the paper's table) and 12.0 in 2007. Use in the past year: 3.4 and 3.7 in 100.

claim.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether decriminalising the possession of all illegal drugs for personal use in Portugal, from cannabis to heroin and cocaine, changed drug use, drug deaths, HIV or the load on police and prisons. The law, in force from 1 July 2001, made acquiring, possessing or using up to ten days' supply an administrative offence dealt with by regional dissuasion commissions (panels of three that can refer people to treatment or impose sanctions such as fines) instead of a crime punishable by up to a year in prison; possession for supply stayed a crime. It came two years after a national drug strategy began expanding prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration (May 1999), and no study read compares Portugal with a modelled counterfactual. In national statistics compiled by two researchers who had studied the reform for years, set beside Spain and Italy where data allowed, without statistical tests (Hughes & Stevens, 2010), the share of people aged 15 to 64 who had ever used an illegal drug rose from 7.8% in 2001 (7.6% in the paper's table) to 12.0% in 2007, while use in the past year went from 3.4% to 3.7% (cannabis 3.3% to 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% to 0.6%, heroin 0.2% to 0.3%); there was no national survey before 2001, the paper does not say when in 2001 the first one was done, and past-year cannabis and cocaine use also rose in Spain and Italy. Among school students aged 15 to 16, lifetime use of any illegal drug was about 12% in 1999, 18% in 2003 and 14% in 2007 (editors' reading of a figure). Estimated problem drug use went from 7.6 to 6.8 per 1,000 people aged 15 to 64 between 2000 and 2005, within overlapping ranges that the authors say make the fall not statistically significant, and estimated injecting drug use from 3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000; both estimates are derived from numbers in treatment, which rose from 23,654 people in 1998 to 38,532 in 2008. New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs fell from 907 in 2000 to 267 in 2008 and new AIDS cases from 506 to 108, a fall the paper says has been attributed primarily to expanded harm reduction, without saying by whom. Recorded drug-related deaths (deaths with a positive post-mortem test for an illegal drug, as the authors define this series in their later paper) went from a peak of 369 in 1999 and 280 in 2001 to about 150 a year in 2002–2004 and about 340 in 2008 (editors' readings of figures), while toxicological autopsies rose from 1,166 in 2002 to 2,805 in 2008; deaths that doctors certified as caused by drugs, a series that starts in 2001, went from about 76 in 2001 to about 9 in 2005 and about 20 in 2008 (editors' readings; Hughes & Stevens, 2012). Criminal drug arrests fell from over 14,000 people in 2000 to 5,000–5,500 a year, mostly because possession for personal use stopped counting as a crime: about 7,600 of the roughly 14,300 people arrested in 2000 were arrested for possession or use, and all police contacts for drug offences, crimes and administrative offences together, were about 10,500 to 12,000 a year after the reform against about 11,400 to 14,300 in 1998–2000 (editors' readings of a figure). The share of prisoners whose offences were drug-related fell from 44% in 1999 to 21% in 2008. Retail prices fell from 2001 (the peak year for heroin; cocaine and hash prices peaked in 2000), as measured from July 2001 by a different method; heroin and cocaine prices in 2008 were similar to those of 1998–1999. The authors state that it is impossible to say that any of these changes was the direct result of decriminalisation, and that expanded treatment and an ageing population of people who use heroin contributed. In a later critique of the two most publicised accounts, a report for the Cato Institute, a US libertarian think tank, that judged the reform a clear success and reports for an association for a drug-free Portugal (APLD) that judged it a clear failure, the same authors, who call themselves participants in the debate, found that each account rested on selected datasets and years, and argue that past-year use and doctor-certified deaths are better guides than lifetime use and toxicology-positive deaths (Hughes & Stevens, 2012; its erratum corrects only a remark on where one cited report could be found). The data end in 2008, with some series to 2009. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claim.population: People in Portugal, in national statistics mostly for 1998–2008: people aged 15 to 64 in the national household surveys of 2001 and 2007; school students (ESPAD, aged 15 to 16, and other school surveys); estimated numbers of people with problem drug use and of people who inject drugs; people who use drugs newly diagnosed with HIV or AIDS; deaths recorded by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine (positive toxicology test) and the National Statistics Institute (certified by doctors, from 2001); people arrested or detected for drug offences; prisoners; with Spain and Italy for some indicators
claim.exposure: Decriminalisation of the acquisition, possession and use of all illegal drugs for personal use (up to ten days' supply), in force from 1 July 2001 under Law 30/2000: an administrative offence handled by regional dissuasion commissions instead of a crime; part of a national drug strategy that expanded prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration from May 1999
claim.comparator: Portugal before July 2001 (late 1990s to 2001, depending on the indicator; no adult survey before 2001 and no doctor-certified death series before 2001); Spain and Italy, which had made drug use an administrative offence in 1992 and 1990, for some indicators; no modelled counterfactual
claim.outcome: Reported drug use (lifetime, past year, past month) among adults and students; estimated problem and injecting drug use; new HIV and AIDS diagnoses among people who use drugs; drug-related deaths (toxicology-positive and doctor-certified); arrests and police contacts for drug offences; drug-related prisoners; retail prices; and what two publicised accounts claimed about these
claim.magnitude: Hughes & Stevens (2010), Portugal, people aged 15–64: lifetime use of any illegal drug 7.8% (text; 7.6% in Table 1) in 2001 and 12.0% in 2007 (+4.4 points by Table 1); past-year 3.4% and 3.7% (+0.3); past-year cannabis 3.3% and 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% and 0.6%, heroin 0.2% and 0.3%, ecstasy 0.4% and 0.4%; Spain past-year cannabis 9.7% and 10.1%, cocaine 2.6% and 3.1%; Italy 6.2% and 14.6%, 1.1% and 2.2%. Students aged 15–16 (ESPAD), lifetime use of any illegal drug 8%, 12%, 18% and 14% in 1995, 1999, 2003 and 2007 (editors' reading). Problem drug use 7.6 (range 6.8–8.5) and 6.8 (6.2–7.4) per 1,000 aged 15–64 in 2000 and 2005; injecting 3.5 (2.3–4.6) and 2.0 (1.8–2.2); Italy, problem drug use 6.0 and 8.6 per 1,000 in 2001 and 2007. People in treatment 23,654 (1998) and 38,532 (2008). New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs 907 (2000) and 267 (2008); AIDS 506 and 108. Recorded drug-related deaths 369 (1999); about 155, 152 and 157 in 2002–2004 and about 339 in 2008 (editors' readings of Figure 7); toxicological autopsies 1,166 (2002) and 2,805 (2008); deaths with opiates as the main substance 95% (1999) and 59% (2008). Criminal drug arrests over 14,000 (2000) and 5,000–5,500 a year after the reform; administrative detections about 6,000 a year; editors' readings of Figure 2: consumer offences about 7,600 of about 14,300 arrests in 2000; trafficking-type arrests about 4,500–6,300 a year in 1998–2000 and 5,200–5,600 in 2001–2008; all police contacts about 11,400–14,300 and 10,500–12,000 a year. Drug-related prisoners 44% (1999) and 21% (2008); prison density 119 (2001) and 101.5 (2005) per 100 places. Retail prices in euros per gram: heroin 38.50, 31.33, 49.72 and 50.27 (1998–2001) and 33.25 (2008); cocaine 45.63, 40.37, 60.31, 53.51 and 45.56. Hughes & Stevens (2012): toxicology-positive deaths (INML) 280 (2001), 216 (2006) and 314 (2007); doctor-certified drug deaths (INE) about 76 (2001), 34, 23, 20, 9 (2005), 12, 14 and 20 (2008) (editors' readings of Figure 4); adults' past-month use about 2.5% in 2001 and 2007; past-year use at 15–24 about 8.3% and 7.0%, at 25–34 about 4.9% and 7.0% (editors' readings of Figures 2 and 3); students' lifetime cannabis use (ESPAD) +60% around the reform, about 9.4% (1999) to 15.0% (2003), then about 13.0% (2007) (editors' readings of Figure 1). Neither paper gives intervals or statistical tests for these changes.
claim.rating_reasoning: Observational evidence (national before-and-after statistics, and a critique that compiles further national series) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, it is very low, the floor. The claim concerns whether the law changed outcomes, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the trends are reported in it as descriptions of the national figures, not rated as a separate claim. Counted once: the 2012 critique is by the same authors, restates the 2010 comparison with Spain and Italy and uses the same toxicology-positive death series; its new data are the doctor-certified death series (INE, from 2001) and re-presented school and adult survey figures, which enter as second-hand national statistics, while its judgements of the two advocacy accounts enter as what it argues. Status contested: credible figures point both ways on whether drug problems eased after 2001 (lifetime use rose, past-year cocaine and heroin use rose by tenths of a point and toxicology-positive deaths returned near the 1999 peak by 2008, while past-year use overall barely changed and estimated injecting, HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs, drug-related prisoners and doctor-certified deaths fell), and the critique changes the reading of the death trend and shows that both publicised accounts rested on selected data, so the six-part debate box applies. The erratum to the 2012 paper (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727, 10.1111/j.1465-3362.2012.00462.x), now read, corrects only the statement that a cited report of the US Office of National Drug Control Policy could not be found on that office's website (p. 111); nothing used here changes. Neither paper has a conflict-of-interest statement; the authors had studied the reform for years, partly in collaboration with the agency that ran it, and wrote one of the accounts in the debate.
claim.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In national statistics up to 2008, Portugal after 2001 saw a rise in the share of adults who had ever used an illegal drug (from about 8 to 12 in 100), little change in past-year use, falls in estimated injecting, in new HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs, in drug-related prisoners and in doctor-certified drug deaths, no rise in police contacts for drug offences, and a fall and then a rise in toxicology-positive deaths that tracks the number of autopsies (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). Neither a clear success nor a clear failure describes this pattern: each publicised account rested on selected surveys and years, and both contained errors identified by the critics, such as a cannabis ranking in which three EU countries were in fact lower and a 40% rise in homicides that covered all homicides, not drug-related ones (Hughes & Stevens, 2012). These figures do not fit the prediction, cited by the authors, that decriminalisation necessarily increases drug use and its harms: past-year use rose by tenths of a point, and HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs and doctor-certified deaths fell, although lifetime use rose by about half (editors' calculation) (Hughes & Stevens, 2010, 2012). But whether the law itself caused any of the changes cannot be told from them, because treatment and harm reduction expanded from 1999, recorded deaths had begun to fall before July 2001 (editors' reading of a figure), and the authors themselves say that none of the changes can be shown to be the direct result of decriminalisation (Hughes & Stevens, 2010). The evidence fits decriminalisation as one part of a package with expanded treatment; it does not show what the law alone did.

questions_now.q: Do results with take-home strips match testing by trained staff?

lines_now.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often.
lines_now.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In 2019, people took strips from ten health sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results, and 5 in 100 on site. The authors think most of the extra take-home positives were false.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.
lines_now.rate: One study in British Columbia in 2019 compared results people recorded themselves with staff results on different samples. People chose which result sheets to hand back, and many readings were recalled later.

freq.title: Out of every 100 crystal meth samples, how many showed fentanyl?

claim.statement: In British Columbia in 2019, take-home testing by people who use drugs (strips from ten harm-reduction sites, used at home on 55 in 100 result sheets, in alleys and streets on 22 and at supervised consumption or overdose prevention sites on 29, more than one setting possible; 218 people returning 336 result sheets) compared with on-site testing of other samples by trained staff at the same sites in the same four months was associated with a similar share of fentanyl-positive results for opioid samples and a much larger share for stimulant samples. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%) against 591 of 663 on site (89.1%), a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9) within the pre-set equivalence margin of ±5 points. Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 (27.6% as printed) against 5 of 97 (5.2%); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); the study was not powered for these. By design no sample was tested both ways, and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, so these are shares of positive results, not accuracy; the authors nonetheless conclude that people can use the strips accurately with minimal training, and think the stimulant excess mostly reflects false positives from how samples were prepared, which was not tested (Klaire et al., 2022). Results were self-reported, about 6 in 10 sheets were filled in from memory at return (by the paper's Table 3; its text gives the reverse), the number of kits handed out and not returned is unknown, and similar shares near 90% can hide reading errors in both directions. A scoping review relays from three US syringe services programme studies that 3% to almost 34% of people had difficulty interpreting results and that some believed the line's strength showed how strong the fentanyl was (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand; its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study, as its complete reference list confirms, and holds only for crystal methamphetamine); a 2018 commentary relays a preliminary study, with design and testers not stated, in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results (McGowan et al., 2018, second-hand); and in a laboratory study of a colour kit, two testers new to it misread known drugs in both directions (Murray et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: People using ten harm-reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, April to July 2019, who took home fentanyl test strips and returned results (218 people, 336 sheets, 1680 strip results)
claim.exposure: Fentanyl test strips used and read by the person wherever they chose to test, after brief peer training
claim.comparator: On-site testing of other samples with the same strips by trained staff at the same sites in the same months (852 samples)
claim.outcome: Share of fentanyl-positive strip results, by the drug the sample was expected to be
claim.magnitude: Opioids: take-home 994/1105 (90.0%) against on-site 591/663 (89.1%); difference 0.8 points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9), equivalent within ±5 (p = 0.00275). Crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed; 27.5% by the counts, editors' calculation) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 (14.8 to 30.1); cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), difference 16.1 (7.1 to 25.1). Settings of take-home use (sheets, more than one possible): home 184 (54.8%), alleys and streets 74 (22.0%), supervised sites 97 (28.9%). Second-hand: difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (Kutscher et al., citing Peiper et al., 2019, Tilhou et al., 2022, and Park et al., 2021); its 'five times more frequent at home' matches this study's crystal methamphetamine figures only (27.6% against 5.2%, 5.3-fold; cocaine about 16-fold; opioids equal; editors' calculation); 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results in a preliminary study (McGowan et al.).
claim.rating_reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down, to the floor of very low. Rated as worded: agreement of shares of positive results between people using take-home strips and staff testing on site, not the accuracy of home testing, which no study read measured; whether home testing changes behaviour is a separate question. Status single study: the review's 'five times' figure is the same study (its reference 66, listed again as 92, is Klaire et al., 2022, by the review's Appendix 1), and Murray et al. concerns a colour kit in a laboratory and only qualifies.

lines_now.short: It makes nerve cells let out three brain chemicals: dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
lines_now.but: How it does this is not fully known. So far we have only read a review about it.
how: Meth makes nerve endings let out dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.
It seems to push them out of their storage sacs and run their pumps in reverse.
The details are not fully known. This comes from a review; we have not read the lab studies yet.
lines_now.rate: Lab and animal studies, known only through one review; the original studies haven't been read yet, so how good they are is unknown.

claim.statement: Methamphetamine raises extracellular dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin by promoting their release from nerve endings, apparently by moving them from storage vesicles into the cytoplasm (through the vesicular transporter VMAT2) and reversing transport through the membrane transporters; the mechanism is not completely understood. claim.outcome: Extracellular dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin; mechanism of release

questions_now.q: Did the US regulator approve MDMA therapy for PTSD in 2024?

lines_now.short: In 2024 the US drug regulator said no to MDMA therapy for PTSD.
lines_now.but: We read the panel's notes, but not the final letter.
how: The regulator's expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show the treatment works.
It voted 10 to 1 that the benefits did not outweigh the risks.
Panel members worried that people knew which pill they had. They doubted the later check too.
The regulator's own staff said no blood tests were done on treatment days.
lines_now.rate: The panel's votes come from the regulator's own documents, but the final decision letter was not read, so the decision and its reasons are known mainly from news reports.

claim.statement: The US Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee, meeting on 4 June 2024 on Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA (midomafetamine) capsules with a psychological intervention for PTSD, voted 9 to 2 that the available data did not show the drug to be effective and 10 to 1 that its benefits, with the FDA's proposed risk-mitigation programme, did not outweigh its risks (the FDA's final summary minutes, approved on 26 July 2024). Members cited functional unblinding, unmanaged expectation bias and selection bias; a follow-up too confounded to show durability; the lack of a factorial design separating the drug from the psychotherapy, and the therapists' unblinding and power of suggestion; and, on safety, missing laboratory, QTc and cardiac data, inadequate data on abuse liability and diversion, hyponatremia and the risk of boundary violations; the two members voting yes weighed the large effect sizes. The FDA reviewers' own briefing document, pre-decisional, had put the same issues to the committee: in MAPP2 94% of the MDMA arm and 75% of the placebo arm guessed their allocation and the in-session monitors could probably tell it too; the only outcome after 18 weeks came from an observational visit the FDA judged not designed to evaluate durability; no study separated the effect of the psychotherapy; the QT assessment was incomplete and phase 3 had no laboratory tests on dosing days; and the sponsor had not recorded positive drug effects such as euphoria as adverse events, against the FDA's advice of 2017, which the reviewers said limited the assessment of abuse potential. The decision itself is known only second-hand: as described in a BMJ news report and two later papers, the FDA declined in August 2024 to approve the application and, according to the company, asked for another phase 3 trial (the month is given by a 2025 commentary citing CNN; the decision letter was not read); the BMJ, published on 13 August 2024, says the decision came before the three phase 2 retractions by Psychopharmacology (see the retraction claim in this section). A 2025 paper, citing news reports and an article in JAMA, calls the vote split, and its unsourced statement that the rejection cited weaknesses in safety documentation and in adverse-event reporting is consistent with the reviewers' briefing but not shown by it. The BMJ also states, without a source, that the research in the three retracted papers did not form part of the application; the FDA's briefing bases efficacy on the phase 3 trials and lists phase 2 studies among the sources of its safety data, without naming the retracted analyses or the study site (MP4) behind the retractions; the sponsor's own briefing document for the committee likewise cites none of the three analyses and lists the phase 2 study MP-4 among the 17 studies supporting the drug's safety but not among the six it pooled for its safety analyses (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). The same document dates the FDA's agreement on the phase 3 design (a Special Protocol Assessment, July 2017) and Breakthrough Therapy Designation (August 2017), the final part of the rolling application to December 2023 and the FDA's filing of it, with Priority Review, to February 2024. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: The US regulatory review of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (2024)
claim.exposure: Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA capsules for PTSD
claim.outcome: The advisory committee's votes and stated reasons and the FDA reviewers' concerns (from the FDA's own documents); the FDA decision as reported second-hand
claim.magnitude: Not a quantity. Advisory committee votes (final summary minutes; 11 voting members): effectiveness, yes 2, no 9, abstain 0; benefit-risk with the FDA's proposed REMS, yes 1, no 10, abstain 0. Decision: declined in August 2024 (second-hand; the month from a 2025 commentary citing a CNN report).
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim about documented events, rated as a description (METHODS §6.3): it starts low. Risk of bias, one level: the committee's votes and reasons and the FDA reviewers' concerns now rest on the FDA's own final summary minutes and briefing document, read in full; but the decision itself, its month, its reasons and what the FDA asked for are known only from a news report, the company's statements as relayed, a commentary citing a CNN report and a qualitative study's background statements citing news reports and an article in JAMA, because the decision letter was not read, and two statements (that the rejection cited weaknesses in safety documentation and adverse-event reporting; that the retracted research was not part of the application) have no source; the claim inherits this weakest necessary link (METHODS §6.3). Inconsistency not rated down: the sources agree on the decision; the minutes' counts (9 to 2 and 10 to 1) match the BMJ's summary, and the 2025 study's split vote is a loose description of them. Indirectness not rated down because the statement says which parts are second-hand. Status single study: the account of the meeting rests on one set of FDA documents, that of the decision on one news report, and the other sources cite news reports. The three retractions, documented by the journal's own notices, are a separate claim since the adjudication of 2026-10-17.
