questions_now.q: Can psilocybin help people quit smoking?
Can psilocybin help people quit smoking?

lines_now.short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.
lines_now.but: There was no comparison group, so no one can tell what psilocybin added to all the counselling.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 15 adults who had smoked for 31 years on average got 15 weeks of counselling and psilocybin two or three times.
Six months on, breath and urine tests confirmed 12 of 15 given psilocybin weren't smoking. Four of those 12 had smoked again at some point.
The psilocybin paper cites 45 to 59 in 100 not smoking after intensive standard treatment. With so few people, 12 of 15 isn't clearly better.
lines_now.rate: One small study: just 15 volunteers, all given psilocybin and lots of counselling, with no comparison group, so nobody can tell what psilocybin itself did.

claim.statement: In adults who smoked at least 10 cigarettes a day and still wanted to quit after several attempts, evidence is insufficient to say whether psilocybin given by a study team within an intensive counselling programme, compared with the same programme without psilocybin (not studied: there was no comparison group), changes how many stop smoking: in one open-label pilot at Johns Hopkins (Johnson et al., 2014), 15 adults (10 men; mean age 51; 14 White) who smoked a mean of 19 cigarettes a day for 31 years and had a mean of 6 earlier quit attempts, recruited through advertisements offering a smoking-cessation treatment involving psilocybin (323 screened by telephone, 27 in person) and unpaid, received a 15-week programme of cognitive behavioural therapy with preparation for the sessions (19 in-person meetings and daily calls for 2 weeks after the quit date), with psilocybin given by the study team on the quit date in week 5, in week 7 and optionally in week 13 (trial conditions: 20 mg/70 kg first, then 30 mg/70 kg by default; the route is not stated in this paper). At 6 months, 12 of 15 (80 in 100; exact 95% interval 52% to 96%, editors' calculation) had not smoked in the previous 7 days by their own report, confirmed by breath carbon monoxide and urine cotinine; 3 of these 12 reported lapses of 1, 4 and 48 cigarettes and a fourth a relapse before stopping again, so the paper reports no smoking after the quit date for 8 of 15 (editors' count; continuous abstinence is not reported as such), and the 3 who did not quit resumed daily smoking after 4, 11 and 22 days. The abstract says this rate substantially exceeds the rates commonly reported for other treatments (typically under 35%). The Discussion compares it with 24.9% to 26.3% (bupropion) and 33.5% to 35.2% (varenicline) in trials with 12 brief counselling meetings and with 17.2% for the counselling programme its own was based on, noting that its participants had substantially more staff contact, and with 45% to 59% at about 6 months in two trials of extended treatment combining bupropion, nicotine replacement and cognitive behavioural therapy, saying its rate was higher; the authors say the results should be interpreted with caution, that no definitive conclusions can be drawn about psilocybin's causal role and that the sample's racial homogeneity and high education may have affected the outcomes, and they call for a randomized trial. With an interval of 52% to 96%, the pilot cannot show that its programme did better than intensive standard treatment, and without a comparison group it cannot separate psilocybin from the counselling, contact and motivation of volunteers who sought out a psilocybin treatment (editors' reading). During the 42 sessions, no clinically significant adverse event needed a physician or medication; 6 of 15 rated fear, fear of insanity or feeling trapped as strong or extreme at some point, all resolved by the end of the session. Funding: the Beckley Foundation and the Heffter Research Institute, on whose board of directors one author sits. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claim.population: Adults who smoked at least 10 cigarettes a day, had made several unsuccessful quit attempts and still wanted to quit, were healthy on screening and had no personal or family history of psychotic or bipolar disorder and no drug dependence other than nicotine in the past 5 years, and who answered advertisements for a psilocybin smoking-cessation treatment at Johns Hopkins (15 enrolled of 323 screened by telephone; 10 men; mean age 51; 14 White; a mean of 19 cigarettes a day for 31 years and 6 earlier quit attempts; Johnson et al., 2014)
claim.exposure: Psilocybin given by the study team in two or three sessions (trial conditions: 20 mg/70 kg on the quit date in week 5, then 30 mg/70 kg by default in week 7 and optionally in week 13, with the lower dose allowed; the route is not stated in this paper; 42 sessions in all) within a 15-week cognitive behavioural smoking-cessation programme with preparation for the sessions, 19 in-person meetings and brief daily calls for 2 weeks after the quit date; participants were told not to use other cessation treatments
claim.comparator: None: the pilot had no comparison group; the authors compare their result with published trials of other treatments in other people (bupropion or varenicline with brief counselling, the counselling programme theirs was based on, and extended treatment combining bupropion, nicotine replacement and cognitive behavioural therapy)
claim.outcome: 7-day point-prevalence abstinence 6 months after the quit date, from timeline follow-back calendars confirmed by breath carbon monoxide (6 ppm or less) and urine cotinine (below 200 ng/mL); lapses (any smoking after the quit date) and relapses (smoking on 7 or more consecutive days); adverse events during the sessions
claim.magnitude: Johnson et al. (2014), 15 people, no comparison group, so no difference between groups can be estimated: 7-day point-prevalence abstinence at 6 months 12/15 (80%; exact 95% interval 51.9% to 95.7%, editors' calculation), self-reported and confirmed by breath carbon monoxide and urine cotinine; lapses of 1, 4 and 48 cigarettes in 3 of the 12 and a relapse in a fourth, leaving 8/15 with no smoking reported after the quit date (editors' count); the 3 who did not quit resumed daily smoking after 4, 11 and 22 days; strong or extreme ratings of fear, fear of insanity or feeling trapped at some point 6/15; no clinically significant adverse event needing a physician or medication in 42 sessions. Rates the Discussion cites from other trials in other people, at about 6 months: 45% to 59% with extended combined treatment, 33.5% to 35.2% with varenicline and 24.9% to 26.3% with bupropion (with 12 brief counselling meetings), and 17.2% with the counselling programme its own was based on.
claim.rating_reasoning: Rated on one open-label pilot without a comparison group (Johnson et al., 2014): non-randomized evidence starts low; down two levels for risk of bias (critical: psilocybin came with intensive counselling and staff contact in volunteers who sought out a psilocybin treatment, and nothing was compared) and one for imprecision (15 people; an interval from 52% to 96%): very low, the lowest level, which either reason alone would reach. 'Evidence is insufficient' because without a comparison there is no estimate of what psilocybin did (METHODS §6.1): the 12 of 15 is reported as what happened to 15 volunteers, not as an effect. The abstract's comparison with other treatments (typically under 35%) is not adopted, because it sets the pilot against other trials in other people with less staff contact, and the Discussion's own figures for extended combined treatment (45% to 59%) fall within the pilot's interval. Status single study: no controlled test of psilocybin for smoking was among the sources read (card sc_johnson_2014). Split from the answer on drinking, which rests on a randomized trial and is rated low on its own, because GRADE rates certainty per outcome. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions.

questions_now.q: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think?

lines_now.short: In one study, story details changed how harshly readers judged the person who died.
lines_now.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.
lines_now.rate: One online experiment in which chance decided which version of a made-up news story 1,248 UK adults read. The plan was not published first, and the stigma questions were new.

claim.statement: In one randomized online experiment with UK adults, details in a simulated news report of a drug death changed how much stigma readers said they felt towards the person who died, by small to moderate amounts, but hardly changed their stated support for harm-reduction policies. In June 2022, 1,248 adults on a UK online research panel (Prolific; mean age 45.7, 51.0% women) were each randomly assigned to read one of eight versions of a BBC-style news story about an inquest, adapted from a real BBC report of an ecstasy death in 2019; the versions differed in the person's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 and had used the drug 'once or twice', or 43 and had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin). Stigma towards the person, on a new nine-item measure of blame, anger, pity, responsibility, control and wish for distance (range 9 to 81), was higher when the person was a man (mean 45.6 against 43.4 for a woman), when the person was older with long use (46.7 against 42.3) and when the drug was heroin (46.9 against 42.1): about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations (editors' calculation), with the eight versions ranging from 38.6 (young woman, ecstasy) to 50.1 (older man, heroin). Support for six harm-reduction policies (such as drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone and opioid agonist treatment; range 6 to 30) was slightly higher after the older person's story (about 23.6 against 23.0, editors' calculation from the condition means, about 0.1 standard deviation; the paper prints the two means in reverse order), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories only (about 23.9 against 22.7, with none in the heroin stories, editors' calculation), and did not differ by drug or by gender. In exploratory, non-randomized analyses of 868 participants, stronger belief in a just world, less perspective-taking and more general stigma towards people with drug problems went with more stigma towards the person, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug death went with less (Sumnall et al., 2023). The study was not registered in advance, the stigma measure was new, the panel was matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented people with degrees and people who prefer left-wing parties, the outcomes were self-reports measured once straight after one written story, and 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'. How real news coverage affects behaviour, policy or the people affected was not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claim.population: UK adults on an online research panel (Prolific), June 2022; 1,248 randomized (mean age 45.7, 51.0% women; matched to the UK on sex, age and ethnicity)
claim.exposure: Reading a simulated news report of a drug death in which the person who died was a man, was 43 with 15 years of regular use, or died after heroin
claim.comparator: Versions of the same report in which the person was a woman, was 21 and had used the drug once or twice, or died after ecstasy (factorial randomization)
claim.outcome: Self-reported stigma towards the person depicted (new nine-item measure) and stated support for six harm-reduction policies, measured once, straight after reading
claim.magnitude: Sumnall et al. (2023), 2 × 2 × 2 factorial, n = 1,248 (degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed). Stigma (9–81): man 45.6 (SD 12.1) against woman 43.4 (12.6), F(1,1230) = 11.1, p < .001; older with 15 years' use 46.7 (11.8) against younger, used once or twice, 42.3 (12.7), F = 40.5, p < .001; heroin 46.9 (11.5) against ecstasy 42.1 (12.8), F = 50.1, p < .001; editors' d about 0.18, 0.36 and 0.39; condition means 38.6 to 50.1. Harm-reduction support (6–30): age, F = 4.5, p = .035 (older about 23.6 against younger 23.0, editors' calculation; d about 0.12); in the ecstasy stories about 23.9 against 22.7 and in the heroin stories 23.3 against 23.3 (editors' calculation from Table 1); the F = 4.8, p = .029 printed with the ecstasy comparison is more consistent with an interaction in an approximate reconstruction (age-by-drug F about 5.4; within-ecstasy age F about 10.1), but rounded Table 1 summaries cover 1,248 assigned participants while the residual degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed under the full eight-cell model, so the exact test identity remains unresolved (editors’ conditional calculation); gender F = .0, p = .802; drug F = .0, p = .922. Exploratory regression (868 participants, editors' calculation from degrees of freedom): story factors R² = .068, final model R² = .569.
claim.rating_reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb 'increases' rests on random assignment within the experiment and applies to stigma towards the depicted person; for support for harm-reduction policies the claim reports a very small difference by age with use history and no difference by drug or gender. The participant-trait associations come from non-randomized regressions on 868 participants and are reported as associations. Status single study; the authors report no earlier experiment on news depictions of drug deaths.

questions_now.q: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?
Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?

lines_now.short: The same drug. People starting crack reported more signs of dependence than people starting powder.
lines_now.but: Each person was asked once, so the surveys cannot show that crack itself is the reason.
how: Powder can't be smoked; crack is smoked. Smoked or injected cocaine peaks in the blood within minutes, snorted cocaine after about half an hour.
In US surveys from 1995 to 1998, about 18 to 32 in 100 people who had just started crack reported each sign of dependence. For people who had just started powder, it was 5 to 12 in 100.
After allowing for how many days people had used, and for age, drinking, smoking and injecting, the gap was smaller but did not go away.
A review of 302 studies found comparisons of crack with other cocaine mixed. Its authors say crack is not a likely direct cause of the infections and violence linked to it.
lines_now.rate: US household surveys from 1995–1998 that asked people once, with no way to know how people differed before they started. A review of 302 articles says the wider research disagrees.

claim.statement: Crack and powder are the same drug in two forms. A 1996 narrative review puts most differences between them down to the route each form allows and the speed and amount of cocaine it delivers, and to the amounts people use, rather than to the form itself; a 2017 systematic review names crack's own pharmacology and routes, and the marginalized circumstances of many people who use it, as possible explanations without testing them. No source read tests crack against powder with route, amount and circumstances accounted for. Powder cannot be smoked because it breaks down at the temperature needed to vaporize it, while the base form (crack) can, so to some extent the form sets the route: crack is smoked, powder is snorted or injected. Once in the blood, the 1996 review describes the two forms as eliminated and broken down alike, with peak levels in venous blood about 5 minutes after smoking or injecting against about 30 to 40 minutes after snorting (second-hand from studies not read here; Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). In US household surveys of 1995–1998, among 762 people who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months, each of seven dependence features was reported more often by the 190 who had started crack (some of whom had also just started powder) than by the 572 who had started powder and never used crack: weighted occurrence in the past year about 18% to 32% against about 5% to 12%, or about 2.5 to 4.4 times as often by the editors' reading of the figure. The summary odds ratio across features, adjusted for sex, age, race, daily drinking, daily tobacco smoking, injecting and the number of days cocaine was used, was 1.9 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.5), and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for a further 93 people who had recently started crack after two or more years of powder use; without the term for days of use the estimate was about 2.3 to 3.7, reported without intervals (Chen & Anthony, 2004). Those estimates come from one interview, with use, form and problems all self-reported and no measure of how people differed before they started; the authors say a greater susceptibility among people who start crack cannot be ruled out, and they fitted the model with and without days of use because dependence itself may raise use, so adjusting for it may remove part of a real difference. The 2017 systematic review of 302 included articles pooled only comparisons of crack use against people not using drugs or the general population, never against powder. In its narrative synthesis, comparisons of people using crack with people using other forms of cocaine were described as mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies), and as showing no difference for 10 other diagnoses (5 studies); single studies found more anorexia and insomnia and less suicidal thinking with crack, and more violence toward others than among people snorting cocaine but not more than among people injecting it; the review neither pooled nor tested these comparisons. Its authors judge crack not a plausible direct cause of the infections and violence linked with its use, reading crack use as a facilitator or marker of risk behaviours and risk environments, and call it unclear for mental health whether crack use is a cause, a consequence or comorbid (Butler et al., 2017). The 1996 review, whose evidence on patterns of use comes from uncontrolled surveys and treatment, street and jail samples, mostly of the mid-1980s to early 1990s, reports that people who smoke or inject cocaine typically use it more often and in larger amounts than people who snort it (one Miami sample found the largest amounts among people snorting), that people who smoke crack reach regular use sooner than people who snort or inject, and that smoking or injecting goes with a faster onset of problems and earlier treatment; its statement that differences disappear once the amount used is held constant rests partly on two sets of meeting proceedings published before crack appeared. No comparison of crack with powder in the sources read adjusts for the amount taken per occasion, for illegal drugs other than cocaine, or for income, housing or the policing people met; the household survey adjusts for daily drinking, daily smoking, injecting and days of use. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claim.population: People in US households, 1995–1998 surveys: 762 who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months (572 powder only; 190 recent crack, some of whom had also just started powder) and 93 who had recently started crack after two or more years of powder use; the samples of a 2017 systematic review of 302 included articles on crack use, mostly marginalized high-risk groups in the USA, Brazil and Canada; the treatment, survey, laboratory and administrative sources of a 1996 narrative review
claim.exposure: Crack (smoked cocaine base), compared with cocaine hydrochloride powder (snorted or injected)
claim.comparator: People who had started powder cocaine and never used crack; in the 2017 review's pooled estimates, people not using drugs or the general population (crack against other forms of cocaine only in its narrative synthesis)
claim.outcome: Dependence features, mental-health and other health outcomes, and patterns of use
claim.magnitude: Chen & Anthony (2004), weighted past-year occurrence of seven dependence features: about 5% to 12% among 572 people who had started powder only; about 18% to 32% among 190 who had recently started crack and about 11% to 33% among 93 who had started crack after two or more years of powder use (the group ranges are the first reader's readings of a figure that prints no values). Unadjusted odds ratios, recent crack against powder only: reduced activities 5.6 (1.9 to 15.9), tolerance 4.8 (1.8 to 12.6), inability to cut down 4.0 (1.9 to 8.7), emotional problems 3.5 (1.6 to 7.7), salience 3.4 (1.5 to 7.7), using more than intended 3.1 (1.4 to 7.0), health problems 3.0 (0.9 to 9.7). Adjusted summary across the seven features: 1.9 (1.4 to 2.5) for recent crack and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for crack after two or more years of powder; about 2.3 to 3.7 without the days-of-use term (no intervals). These are odds ratios although the paper calls them relative risks; from the figure the corresponding prevalence ratios are about 2.5 to 4.4 for recent crack and about 1.5 to 3.3 for crack after powder (editors' calculation from the figure readings). Butler et al. (2017): no pooled crack-versus-powder estimate; 12 studies mixed and 5 showing no difference, none pooled or tested by the review; one study found more violence toward others with crack than with snorted cocaine, and no difference from injected cocaine. Hatsukami & Fischman (1996), second-hand: two thirds of people smoking crack used daily against 18% of people snorting powder, among people interviewed in treatment, street, jail or prison settings in New York City in 1988–1989; in the 1991 national survey, crack use was 52.5% among people who used cocaine frequently and 17.5% among those who used it infrequently (neither defined), injecting 24.3% against 9.3%.
claim.rating_reasoning: Observational evidence starts low. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 and indirectness −1 take it below the floor: very low. The claim is worded as an association and is rated as one (METHODS §6.3). Status mixed: a population survey finds an excess of dependence features with crack that shrinks after adjustment, while the one systematic review covering the same question describes the comparisons as mixed and pools none, and the 1996 review attributes the differences to route, amount and context without testing them. The three sources are not independent: the 2017 review includes Chen & Anthony (2004) in its narrative synthesis and cites the 1996 review as background, so they are counted once. Not used, following the study cards: a causal effect of smoking crack, the 1996 review's figures as measurements, its gateway reading of sequence data, and any crack-versus-powder difference in physical harms, for which the sources read give only second-hand, unadjusted figures.

questions_now.q: How many people who use stimulants like meth become dependent?

lines_now.short: An old US survey asked people who had used stimulants like meth. About 11 in 100 had been dependent at some point.
lines_now.but: Neither survey gives a number for meth alone. The US one also counted people who had only just started.
how: In the early 1990s, a US survey used set interview questions to find who had ever been dependent on a drug they had used.
Stimulants other than cocaine: about 11 in 100. Tobacco 32, alcohol 15, cocaine 17.
It counted people who had just started, so they had little time to become dependent.
An Australian survey asked in a different way. It estimated about 50 in 100 within 14 years, also counting a related diagnosis called 'abuse'.
lines_now.rate: Two household surveys, in the US in 1990 to 1992 and Australia in 2007. The US one lumped meth with other stimulants, prescription pills included, and the Australian one never said which stimulants.

freq.what: of people who had used stimulants other than cocaine had been dependent at some point
freq.note: US survey, 1990 to 1992: stimulants other than cocaine, not meth alone. Tobacco was measured differently.
freq.compare_k: For comparison, in the same survey:

claim.statement: The US National Comorbidity Survey (1990–1992; household sample aged 15–54; structured CIDI interview) reported, for each drug class separately, the proportion of people who had ever used it who had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for dependence, with non-medical use of stimulants other than cocaine counted as one class. Among people who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically (15.3% of the population; dextroamphetamine and methamphetamine are the examples given), 11.2% (SE 1.6; about 8.1% to 14.3%, editors' calculation) had ever met the criteria, against 31.9% for tobacco (no standard error; tobacco use came from a separate 1991 survey and dependence was assessed for daily smoking in a subsample), 15.4% for alcohol, 16.7% for cocaine, 23.1% for heroin and 9.1% for cannabis. Such proportions are taken at a single interview among everyone who had ever used, including once (the dependence questions were asked only of people reporting more than a few occasions of use), and do not account for people who started recently; the data are three decades old, grouped across stimulants and based on DSM-III-R criteria. The source calls the class psychostimulants other than cocaine; it includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants. A 2007 Australian national household survey (8,841 people aged 16–85; response 60%; WMH-CIDI 3.0 interview) measured something different. Its outcome was broader, DSM-IV stimulant abuse or dependence, in a stimulant class the paper does not define. Of 579 people who had used stimulants, 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) had met the criteria by the interview. A survival analysis, which uses the years since each person first used and so allows for people who had started recently, estimated a cumulative probability of 50.4% (no interval given) of developing the disorder within 14 years of first use, 12.2% within the first year. The criteria were asked only of people who had used at least five times, and the authors note that counting abuse as well as dependence gives higher estimates than studies of dependence alone. The two surveys therefore measure different quantities and cannot be compared directly, and neither gives a figure for methamphetamine alone.
claim.population: US household (noninstitutionalized) population aged 15–54 in 1990–1992 who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically; Australian household population aged 16–85 in 2007 who had ever used stimulants (class not defined)
claim.exposure: lifetime extramedical use of psychostimulants other than cocaine, including prescription stimulants used without or beyond a prescription (US); lifetime use of stimulants, class not defined (Australia)
claim.outcome: lifetime DSM-III-R dependence, as a proportion at interview (US); lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence, as a proportion at interview and as a cumulative probability by years since first use (Australia)
claim.magnitude: US NCS (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): proportion ever dependent (DSM-III-R) among people who had ever used extramedically: psychostimulants other than cocaine 11.2% (SE 1.6; editors' 95% CI about 8.1% to 14.3%), from 15.3% lifetime use and 1.7% lifetime dependence in the population; tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6). Stimulants by age: 13.5% (15–24), 13.9% (25–34), 7.7% (35–44), 6.5% (45–54); by sex: men 9.7%, women 13.3% (Tables 4–5). Australia 2007 (NSMHWB; weighted; stimulant class not defined; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8) of 579 people who had used stimulants had ever met the criteria at interview; cumulative probability by years since first use (discrete-time survival analysis, no interval) 12.2% within the first year and 50.4% within 14 years; among those who developed the disorder, half did so within about 3 years (IQR 1–5) of first use.
claim.rating_reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions and a cumulative probability in survey populations): starts low. Risk of bias, one level, for the Australian figures only (60% response, recalled timing, unclear denominator); the US figures are not downgraded (JBI low; the authors discuss frame, deaths and self-report, pp. 263–265). Indirectness, two levels: neither survey isolates methamphetamine, the US class includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants, and the Australian class is undefined and its outcome includes abuse; the criteria are DSM-III-R (1990–1992) and DSM-IV (2007). Not downgraded for inconsistency, because the two figures measure different things: a proportion ever dependent among everyone who had ever used, at one interview, against a projected cumulative probability of abuse or dependence by 14 years after first use. Certainty very low. The tobacco proportion is less comparable than the others: it combines tobacco use from a separate 1991 survey with dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample, and has no standard error. Status single study: the two surveys measure different quantities (see inconsistency), so they neither replicate nor contradict each other, and each figure rests on one survey; the four- to five-fold gap between them has candidate explanations (abuse counted, undefined class, a denominator that may exclude people with few uses, country and decade) that have not been tested. Imprecision not downgraded: the US proportion has a standard error and the Australian 45.7% an interval; the 50.4% has none, so its precision cannot be judged, which changes nothing at the floor. The US authors conclude from their figures that many, perhaps most, people who use a drug do not become dependent (p. 265); for stimulants, the Australian survival estimate (about half within 14 years, abuse included) shows that this conclusion depends on the measure and on how the outcome is defined.

questions_now.q: Why does taking more raise blood levels more than expected?

lines_now.short: A bigger dose of MDMA raised blood levels by more than the dose itself rose.
lines_now.but: Only 8 men were compared, in a lab, and the study was not planned to look at this.
how: In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total over the day.
Outside the kidneys, MDMA was cleared about half as fast at the larger dose. The authors read this as slower breakdown in the liver.
The authors suggest the breakdown gets saturated or that MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. They also say people may be more prone to acute toxicity; toxicity was not measured.

Feeling little from an amount can come from a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a muting medicine or bodies that differ, and some people take more. These studies gave fixed amounts, so they did not test that.
lines_now.rate: One lab trial in which each of 8 men was his own comparison. Blood was tested directly, but this analysis was added afterwards, and with so few men the extra rise could be chance.

claim.statement: In eight men given MDMA 75 mg and 125 mg on separate days in a randomized, double-blind crossover, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.81 times higher (236.4 against 130.9 ug/L) and a 24-hour exposure 1.97 times higher (2623.7 against 1331.5 ug x h/L), so blood levels rose more than the dose did (de la Torre et al., 2000; ratios from the printed means). Clearance outside the kidneys fell from 74.0 to 38.1 L/h while clearance by the kidneys did not change, and across the five dose levels from 50 to 150 mg, with different men at 50, 100 and 150 mg, the same eight men at 75 and 125 mg, and only two men at each of the lowest and highest, the 24-hour exposure ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug x h/L, so differences between men are mixed in with the dose. The authors give two explanations, saturation of MDMA's breakdown (which they say cannot be excluded) and MDMA's blocking of the enzyme CYP2D6 that breaks it down, and state that the observations were retrospective and the studies were not designed to detect this. The authors' abstract goes further, concluding that this holds for the whole population whatever the CYP2D6 genotype and that small increases in the amount taken give disproportionate rises in blood level, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity; the dose comparison was made in men with normal CYP2D6 only and no toxicity outcome was measured. In a later study of 15 men, one dose of MDMA switched CYP2D6 off, and the enzyme's activity had not fully recovered after 10 days (O'Mathúna et al., 2008); this fits the second explanation, as does the small difference between people with and without a working enzyme (Schmid et al., 2016). The authors of the 2008 study infer, without giving a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts the effect, bodies that differ) and some take more. None of these studies tested people who took more because they felt little: the amounts were fixed and given to healthy men in a laboratory, and what they show is that a larger single amount gave a larger rise in blood level than the amount itself. Second doses taken 2 or 24 hours after a first are covered in the library's separate claim on acute tolerance.
claim.population: Healthy adult men with earlier MDMA experience in laboratory studies: 14 men (8 in a randomized crossover at 75 and 125 mg; 6 in a pilot at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and, for the mechanism, 15 men in a probe-drug study
claim.exposure: A larger single dose of MDMA (study conditions: 75 mg and 125 mg, and 50, 100 and 150 mg in the pilot, by mouth)
claim.comparator: The same eight men at the smaller dose, with dose-normalized exposure as the yardstick
claim.outcome: Peak and 24-hour exposure of MDMA in plasma, dose-normalized exposure, kidney and non-kidney clearance, and recovery of urinary MDMA and HMMA
claim.magnitude: 75 mg against 125 mg, 8 men (de la Torre et al., 2000): peak 130.9 (SD 38.6) against 236.4 (58.0) ug/L; AUC(0-24 h) 1331.5 (646.0) against 2623.7 (572.9) ug x h/L; dose-normalized AUC 17.8 (8.6) against 21.0 (4.6), paired t test of AUC(0-infinity) P<0.03, 90% interval of the within-person ratio -0.3 to 89.3%; non-renal clearance 74.0 against 38.1 L/h (P<0.03); total clearance 86.9 (74.4) against 51.1 (14.1) L/h as printed; unchanged MDMA in urine 71.2 (13.7) against 169.6 (69.5) micromol. Across 50 to 150 mg, 24-hour exposure 100.1 and 813.9 (two men at 50 mg) against 5132.8 and 5232.0 (two men at 150 mg); Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized exposure P<0.1. Editors' calculation from the printed means: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the exposure.
claim.rating_reasoning: The 75 against 125 mg comparison is a randomized, double-blind, within-person crossover and starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -2 (eight men, an interval reaching zero, two men per dose in the wider range) give very low. Status single-study: one study shows the dose comparison; the probe-drug and genotype studies bear on the mechanism, not on dose proportionality. The claim describes the blood levels in fixed-dose laboratory conditions; it is not guidance on any amount.
